hotspot_comment: Land preparation and planting of cereal crops for the 2026/2027 agricultural season are set to begin in October. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_2-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the October–December 2026 period indicates a significant moisture deficit across the entire southern and central regions, stretching up along the northern coastal strip; conversely, only the interior northern and northeastern provinces are projected to receive near-average to above-average precipitation. As reported by [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=AGO] FAO GIEWS (03/09), this dry outlook is heavily influenced by the ongoing El Niño event, which emerged in June and is typically associated with suppressed rainfall totals across much of Southern Africa. Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

Season A planting of crops such as sorghum, maize and beans is about to start under below-average rainfall conditions. However, Burundi is forecast to receive El Niño-related above-average rainfall during the October–December (OND) rainy season, as indicated by the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] seasonal forecasts from the Copernicus Climate Change Service. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/burundi/wfp-burundi-country-brief-september-2026] WFP, the 2026B harvest improved market supplies in Burundi and prices remained broadly stable in August 2026, but most staples stayed above their five-year average, and the gradual depletion of household stocks, high inflation and fuel supply risks could weaken household access to food during the upcoming lean season.
Not a hotspot country according to the latest ASAP analysis.

Poor crop production is expected across Kenya’s North Rift and parts of western Kenya following prolonged dry spells and severe rainfall deficits during critical crop-development stages. [https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/fews.net/east-africa/kenya/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026?utm_source=chatgpt.com__;!!DOxrgLBm!GvWpxNNoS3o2bepAZH_wm1CK821qFcTUlevYiAwCBQeeT2zfJo6y8aXbCUtXWXbk7FEwl4O3dKctNya28rzaGf7GTIYHLqrggBGJ$" target="_blank] FEWSNET estimates long-rains maize production at 22–28% below the five-year average nationally, with production in key North Rift counties including Uasin Gishu, Elgeyo-Marakwet, Nandi and Trans Nzoia estimated at around 43% below the five-year average. Government assessments also report widespread crop failure in the North Rift, with significant losses reported in Uasin Gishu, Trans Nzoia, Bungoma and parts of Kakamega. The Government has subsequently announced plans to import 25 million bags of maize to address the anticipated national supply deficit. Looking ahead, forecasts of a strong El Niño for the upcoming short rains season point to above average rainfall. It is important however to bear in mind that high intensity rainfall will not be immediately beneficial to drought affected crop areas and that there is a high risk of adverse impacts including increased risk of flooding. These conditions could further affect agricultural production, disrupt livelihoods, and complicate recovery efforts in areas already impacted by the current dry spell.

Land preparation and planting of cereal crops for the 2026/2027 agricultural season are set to begin in October. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_2-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the October–December 2026 period indicates a significant moisture deficit nationwide. This grim outlook aligns with the [https://fews.net/southern-africa/lesotho/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026] FEWS NET (August 2026) report, which warns that a projected El Niño event will trigger a late and below-average start to the rainy season, which is expected to delay land preparation, hamper early crop establishment, and restrict agricultural labor opportunities. Given these compounding factors, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

In Madagascar, apart from areas where secondary rice is growing, there are no cereals growing now and in the central and northern areas, the next rice season is expected to start in November with the arrival of the rainy season, which is forecast drier than average in the west in November and December and across the country in January by the C3S multimodel seasonal forecast.In the Grand South (Anosy, Androy and Atsimo Andrefana), the next cereals and legumes season should start in October under forecast drier than average conditions in the western part (Atsimo Andrefana) from November to February according to the C3S multimodel seasonal forecast.The Grand South is estimated to have about 1.5 to 2.0 million people facing acute food insecurity (IPC phase 3 and above) as a result of extreme events (droughts in 2020, 2021 and 2022, cyclones), poor socio economic conditions and aid reduction according to the latest [https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1161004/?iso3=MDG] IPC analysis [https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1161004/?iso3=MDG] and FEWS-NET.

Land preparation and planting of cereal crops for the 2026/2027 agricultural season are set to begin in October. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_2-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the October–December 2026 period indicates a significant moisture deficit across central and southern Malawi, whereas the northern region is projected to receive near-average precipitation. This grim outlook aligns with the [https://fews.net/southern-africa/malawi/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026] FEWS NET (August 2026) report, which warns that a projected strong El Niño event, expected to persist through at least January 2027, will trigger below-average and poorly distributed rainfall at the onset of the rainy season. Consequently, these compounding climate risks are highly likely to suppress agricultural labor demand, reduce planting levels, hamper crop development, and deteriorate pasture and water availability across the most severely affected central and southern zones ([https://fews.net/southern-africa/malawi/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026] FEWS NET, August 2026). Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

Planting of summer cereal crops in the main northern producing provinces is set to begin in November. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_3-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the November–December 2026 period indicates a high probability of below-average precipitation nationwide. This grim outlook aligns with warnings from the Namibia Meteorological Service and independent forecasters, who note that the country is bracing for a hotter and drier rainy season driven by a strengthening El Niño event starting in October 2026. According to [https://www.namibian.com.na/namibia-warned-not-to-wait-for-el-nino-crisis/] The Namibian, this climate shock threatens to trigger widespread water and food insecurity, slash rainfall by up to 150mm across central and northern regions, and place severe pressure on both the national health and livestock sectors. Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

Season A planting of crops such as sorghum, maize and beans is about to start under below-average rainfall conditions. Iburasirazuba (Eastern Province) recorded no rainfall during the last 30 days, compared with a long-term average of 48 mm. However, Rwanda is forecast to receive El Niño-related above-average rainfall during the October–December (OND) rainy season, as indicated by the [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] seasonal forecasts from the Copernicus Climate Change Service. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/rwanda/wfp-rwanda-country-brief-september-2026] WFP, the average cost of the food basket in Rwanda rose by 4 percent in August 2026 compared with July and by 9 percent year-on-year, as broader inflationary pressures and high transport and energy costs outweighed the easing effect of recent harvests and further eroded refugees' purchasing power.

Land preparation and planting of cereal crops for the 2026/2027 agricultural season are set to begin in October. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_2-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the October–December 2026 period indicates a significant moisture deficit nationwide. This grim outlook aligns with the [https://www.fao.org/giews/countrybrief/country.jsp?code=SWZ] FAO GIEWS (25/08) report, which warns that the prevailing El Niño event poses a downside risk to production through drier-than-average conditions. Close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

While most of the country remains in the off-season, rainfall over the past 30 days has been generally average. In the bimodal areas (the northern coastal belt, northeastern highlands, Lake Victoria basin and northern Kigoma), where the Vuli season is about to start, precipitation is [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast.php?sfreg=africa] forecast to be above average over the coming months as a result of the current El Niño episode, and these conditions could favour crop establishment. However, the T[https://dailynews.co.tz/what-above-average-rainfall-really-means-as-2026-vuli-season-nears/] anzania Meteorological Authority (TMA) warns of possible periods of excessive soil moisture and flooding in these areas that could damage crops and agricultural infrastructure. According to [https://reliefweb.int/report/united-republic-tanzania/wfp-tanzania-country-brief-september-2026] WFP, Tanzania's food security situation remains broadly stable thanks to favourable 2025/2026 harvests, with food crop production estimated at 25.2 million tonnes, 6 percent above the previous season. However, food insecurity persists in 14 councils, 13 of which face potential deficits for a second consecutive year.

Rainfall has been below average in the first two dekads of September in most parts of the bimodal areas, signalling a slight delay in the start of the second crop season. In unimodals areas of Karamoja, poor and inconsistent rainfall from June to August together with high temperatures, a pointer to low harvest expectations. According to [https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/fews.net/east-africa/uganda__;!!DOxrgLBm!GvWpxNNoS3o2bepAZH_wm1CK821qFcTUlevYiAwCBQeeT2zfJo6y8aXbCUtXWXbk7FEwl4O3dKctNya28rzaGf7GTIYHLl0uwfyM$" target="_blank] FEWSNET the increased refugee numbers in Karamoja, together with the poor harvest and high food prices contributes to rapidly increasing humanitarian needs. IPC analysis covering 60 areas estimates that approximately 3.6 million people are experiencing Crisis-level food insecurity or worse (IPC Phase 3+) between July 2026 and January 2027, a 6% increase compared with 2025.

Land preparation and planting of cereal crops for the 2026/2027 agricultural season are set to begin in late October. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_2-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the October–December 2026 period indicates a significant moisture deficit nationwide. This grim outlook aligns with the [https://fews.net/southern-africa/zambia/food-security-outlook-update/august-2026] FEWS NET (August 2026) report, which warns that a projected very strong El Niño event will cause a delayed start and below-average precipitation during the 2026/27 rainy season, which are expected to severely reduce planting levels and suppress agricultural labor opportunities. Given these compounding factors, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.

Planting of summer cereal crops is set to begin in November. The [https://agricultural-production-hotspots.ec.europa.eu/seasonal_forecast/monthly-precipitation/forecast/monthly-percentile-probability-plot/multimod-2026_2026_09_3-4-africa.png] Copernicus C3S Multimodel seasonal rainfall forecast for the November–December 2026 period indicates a high probability of below-average precipitation nationwide. This grim outlook aligns with reports from [https://fews.net/southern-africa/zimbabwe/key-message-update/september-2026/print] FEWS NET (September), which warn that a projected El Niño event will cause an erratic start to Zimbabwe's November-to-March rainy season and suppress moisture totals. In response to these climate threats, the government approved a six-pillar mitigation plan in September 2026 to stabilize the Strategic Grain Reserve, secure basic food imports, and support national crop and livestock production ([https://farmfutureafrica.co.zw/zimbabwes-six-pillar-super-el-nino-strategy-what-farmers-need-to-know/] Farm Future Africa). Consequently, close monitoring of the situation over the coming months remains crucial.
